Affiliation:: School of Computer Science, University of Oklahoma
Research Domains: Java Virtual Machine (JVM) / Concurrent Java Threads
Techniques Used: Controlled Empirical Evaluation (using synthetically generated threads)
Key Research Thinking Patterns: Model-Driven Prediction: Developing analytical formulas to forecast system performance and resource availability before execution. (e.g., Co-authoring models to predict the CPU availability for concurrent Java threads and to forecast the performance of compute-intensive tasks on GPUs, allowing a scheduler to make informed decisions prior to task assignment).

Bounding Analysis: Establishing theoretical best-case (upper) and worst-case (lower) limits for performance metrics rather than a single value. (e.g., Deriving "upper- and lower-efficiency bounds" for multi-core processing, acknowledging that actual performance will fall within this range depending on dynamic factors like task scheduling order).

Empirical Validation and Refinement: Using real-world data from benchmarks and simulations to rigorously test, validate, and improve theoretical models. (e.g., Conducting "extensive experimental studies" with thousands of test runs, using the results to confirm the theoretical bounds and develop "sharpened" or average-case prediction models).

Composite Modeling: Integrating models of individual, isolated resources (like CPU or memory) into a single, holistic model to capture their interdependencies. (e.g., Progressing from a CPU-only model to later "derive a composite model" that non-trivially combines both CPU availability and memory models, acknowledging that overall efficiency is a product of multiple competing resources).
Summary Description: Dr. John K. Antonio specializes in Performance Prediction and Modeling, focusing on the execution efficiency of Multi-core Processing and Distributed Systems. His research explores performance forecasting for compute-intensive tasks on both CPUs and GPUs. He applies Analytical Modeling to derive theoretical Upper and Lower Bounds for resource availability, leading to the development of Composite Prediction Models that integrate CPU and memory efficiency. These models are validated through extensive Empirical Studies and Simulation. Significant contributions include enhancing Dynamic Scheduling Robustness against model errors, enabling optimized load balancing, and improving task assignment in heterogeneous environments.
